title: The fourth answer: understanding is Brahman
theme: The formula repeats a last time with vijñāna, understanding — the knowing self. Bhṛgu returns once more, and one more round of austerity leads him to the answer of 3.6.

words.role: subject of the equation inside the quotation
main verb (completing taptvā of the previous anuvāka)
gives the reason for his conclusion
first verb of the third clause
second verb of the third clause

words.context: Śaṅkara takes the equation as praise of the means: austerity is the best means to knowing Brahman

words.role: prior action; completed in the next anuvāka

sandhi.rule: A final m becomes anusvāra before a consonant, P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः); brahma + iti → brahmeti, P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः).
The final t becomes d before a voiced sound, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते), and the following h may become the voiced aspirate dh, P. 8.4.62 (झयो होऽन्यतरस्याम्); hi + eva → hyeva, P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि).
u before a dissimilar vowel becomes v: P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि).
prayanti + abhi-: P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि). abhisaṃviśanti + iti → -īti: P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः).
A final t becomes d before a voiced consonant: P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते).
punaḥ ends in an original r, which reappears before a vowel: punar eva.

sandhi.type: visarga before a voiced consonant; guṇa
sandhi.rule: bhagavaḥ before the voiced b: the visarga becomes u, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च), and a + u gives o, P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः). brahma + iti → brahmeti, also by P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः).
As bhagavo brahmeti: P. 6.1.114 (हशि च) and P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः).

sandhi.type: saḥ before a consonant; aḥ before a
sandhi.rule: saḥ loses its ending before a consonant, P. 6.1.132 (एतत्तदोः सुलोपोऽकोरनञ्समासे हलि). tapaḥ before a: the visarga becomes u, P. 6.1.113 (अतो रोरप्लुतादप्लुते), a + u → o, and the following a is absorbed, P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति), written with avagraha.
The visarga becomes s before t: P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः).

morphology.note: Imperfect of vi-√jñā (ninth class, stem jānā-), with the augment a after the preverb: vi + a-jānāt → vyajānāt. It supplies the main verb for the absolutive taptvā that ended the previous anuvāka.
vi-jñāna, ‘understanding, discernment’: Rāmānanda takes it as the self made of understanding of 2.4 («विज्ञानम् इह विज्ञानमयकोशः»); Gopālānanda as the individual self («विज्ञानम् अत्र जीवः»).

translation.literal: [Having practised austerity,] he understood: ‘Understanding is Brahman.’ For from understanding, indeed, surely, these beings are born; by understanding, born, they live; into understanding they go forth [and] enter. Having understood that, he approached [his] father Varuṇa once more: ‘Teach [me] Brahman, venerable one.’ He said to him: ‘By austerity seek to know Brahman. Austerity is Brahman.’ He practised austerity. Having practised austerity —
translation.readable: Having practised austerity, he understood that understanding is Brahman: for it is from understanding that these beings are born, by understanding that they live once born, and into understanding that they pass and merge at the end. Having understood this, he went to his father Varuṇa again and said, ‘Sir, teach me Brahman.’ Varuṇa told him: ‘Seek to know Brahman by austerity. Austerity is Brahman.’ He practised austerity, and when he had practised it —

syntax: The same frame as 3.2–3.4, with the four case forms of vijñāna. The open ending sa tapas taptvā is completed in 3.6 by ānando brahmeti vyajānāt.

ambiguities.note: Rāmānanda: the self made of understanding of the second vallī («विज्ञानम् इह विज्ञानमयकोशः»). Gopālānanda (modern): the individual self («विज्ञानम् अत्र जीवः»). Kūranārāyaṇa reads it as the totality of individual selves, which scripture and smṛti make the womb of all beings («पुरुषसमष्टेः सर्वयोनित्वं श्रुतिस्मृतिसिद्धम्»), citing the Gītā’s ‘higher nature’.
Rāmānanda: understanding too is found to undergo change («विज्ञानस्य विकारवत्वावगमो हि सन्तोषाभावहेतुः»); still, Bhṛgu went back out of faith in his teacher’s word («गुरुवाक्यश्रद्धातिशयात्»).

metre.name: prose
metre.note: Prose (brāhmaṇa style) in short clauses, divided at the daṇḍas.

beginner: Now Bhṛgu decides that understanding — the knowing self, the one who is aware and decides — is Brahman. This is the closest he has come: every experience and every act seems to come from a knower, to depend on a knower, and to end in a knower. Yet he goes back to his father one more time. One commentator says he noticed that even understanding changes; another says he went back simply because he trusted his teacher. The reply is the same as always: practise austerity. This is the last round. In the next section he will find the answer that does not send him back: bliss.
analogy: A climber who reaches what looks like the summit and sees one more ridge beyond it: the view is real, but it is not yet the top.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: Bhṛgu concludes that understanding is Brahman, because beings are born of it, live by it and go into it. He returns, asks again, and is again told to seek Brahman by austerity.

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Rāmānanda: the self made of understanding of the second vallī («विज्ञानम् इह विज्ञानमयकोशः»). Gopālānanda (modern): the individual self («विज्ञानम् अत्र जीवः»). Kūranārāyaṇa: the collective of individual selves, the womb of all beings according to scripture and smṛti («पुरुषसमष्टेः सर्वयोनित्वं श्रुतिस्मृतिसिद्धम्»), for which he cites the Gītā’s ‘higher nature’ that upholds the world.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Rāmānanda: understanding too is seen to change («विज्ञानस्य विकारवत्वावगमो हि सन्तोषाभावहेतुः»), and Bhṛgu returned to the same practice out of great faith in his teacher’s word («गुरुवाक्यश्रद्धातिशयात्»).

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara, at the next anuvāka: purified by austerity and not finding the full mark of Brahman in breath and the rest, Bhṛgu entered inward step by step and knew the innermost bliss as Brahman («शनैः शनैः अन्तरनुप्रविश्य अन्तरतममानन्दं ब्रह्म विज्ञातवान्»).

commentary.q: What do the forms tell us?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: vijñāna is a neuter a-stem like anna, so the case forms follow 3.2 exactly. The four candidates of 3.2–3.5 — food, breath, mind, understanding — follow the order of the first four selves of the second vallī.

advaita.text: Understanding is still an inner sheath, not the innermost; the austerity continues until the mark of Brahman is found complete («यावद्ब्रह्मणो लक्षणं निरतिशयं न भवति, यावच्च जिज्ञासा न निवर्तते, तावत्तप एव ते साधनम्»), which happens with bliss.

visistadvaita.text: Understanding is the individual self or the collective of selves, real and the womb of beings («पुरुषसमष्टेः सर्वयोनित्वं श्रुतिस्मृतिसिद्धम्»), but distinct from Brahman, who is its inner self; Bhṛgu therefore goes one step further.

dvaita.text: Viṣṇu is called ‘understanding’ because he discerns («विज्ञानं तु विवेचनात्»); it is one more of his names that Bhṛgu came to know.

schools.disagreement: For Śaṅkara the knowing self is still a sheath to be passed through; for the Viśiṣṭādvaita commentators it is the real individual self, distinct from Brahman within it; for Madhva ‘understanding’ is a name of Viṣṇu as the discerner.

parallels.note: The self made of understanding lies within the self made of mind in the Brahmānandavallī; Bhṛgu’s fourth step is the same.

contemporary.text: It is natural to identify with the one who knows and decides — the observer behind experience. The passage treats even that as one more layer, and keeps the search open. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Who is it that notices your thoughts?
reflect.deeper: If the knower changes — learns, forgets, sleeps — can it be the final source of everything?
reflect.practice: Before sleep tonight, notice the moment the sense of ‘I am thinking’ fades.

references.text: Kūranārāyaṇa’s note on this anuvāka ends by pointing ahead to the self made of bliss and the Brahmasūtra’s reading of -maya as ‘abounding’.

flags.note: Whether vijñāna is the self made of understanding (Rāmānanda), the individual self (Gopālānanda) or the collective of selves (Kūranārāyaṇa).
